newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire's Mobutu a textbook master of the powergame.
newsitem.headline: Zaire's Mobutu a textbook master of the powergame.

text.p: President Mobutu Sese Seko, who returns to Zaire on Tuesday after months of medical treatment in Europe, is Africa's longest serving strongman, clinging to power with a mix of military might and political acumen.
In the process, he has given the chaotic country of 40 million people spreading over a vast swathe of Central Africa a badly needed focus for more than three decades.
Accused of being everything from a dictator to a thief, Mobutu has managed to stay in power by keeping his opponents in disarray or buying off his enemies.

Equally adept at exploiting the West's strategic fears, he began a careful process of rehabilitation with key donors -- France, Belgium and the United States -- after they deserted him for five years over lack of democracy and human rights.

The 1994 Rwanda massacres of minority Tutsis, followed by the exodus to Zaire of over a million Rwandan Hutus fearing reprisals, helped bring about a partial thaw as Mobutu's cooperation helped ease a humanitarian nightmare.

Before the thaw, visa problems prevented Mobutu travelling to the West. France barred him from visiting his villa in the Riviera but softened its stance after he cooperated with a French military expedition to halt the killings in Rwanda.
After a controversial Mobutu visit in April 1996, France announced it would restart aide to Kinshasa after a five-year freeze, triggered by human rights concerns.

Adopting a leopard-skin cap and bird-handled ebony cane as his trademarks, the 66-year-old former journalist turned soldier ruthlessly obliterated his opponents when the former Belgian Congo descended into chaos after independence.

He solidified his grip with a system of economic and political patronage that made millionaires of his close associates. Most other Zaireans remained mired in poverty despite their country's vast mineral wealth.
The word "kleptocracy" -- meaning a bureaucracy in which corruption is endemic -- was coined to describe Zaire.
Mobutu seized power in November 1965 after Zaire, then known as Congo Leopoldville, had been ravaged by five years of civil which started after independence from Belgium.
Despite human rights abuses and using his position for personal enrichment Mobutu became the darling of the United States and other Western powers as a buffer against the Communist bloc.

Washington relied on Zaire as a supply route for the U.S.-backed National Union for the Total Independence of Angola (UNITA) rebel movement fighting a 17-year guerrilla war against the Marxist government of neighbouring Angola.
Mobutu's usefulness to Washington faded as the war neared a peaceful settlement and Soviet influence declined in Africa.
Under pressure to make reforms, the Zairean leader opened a Pandora's box when he permitted multi-party politics in April 1990 after more than two decades of single-party rule.
At the same time, the mineral-based economy collapsed as production from vital copper mines in the south plummeted.

Mobutu angered his Western backers, particularly Belgium, when elite troops attacked a student hostel in May 1990, killing dozens and possibly more than 100 students, according to diplomats and church sources. Belgium cut aid in response.

Mobutu's sacking in December 1992 of reformist Prime Minister Etienne Tshisekedi, a one-time ally turned enemy, and the intimidation of the pro-democracy parliament by elite DSP troops brought rebukes from Zaire's main backers.

But shrewd political manoeuvring by Mobutu managed to neutralise the groundswell of political support for Tshisekedi that followed his sacking. A threat by the interim parliament to impeach the president came to nothing.
Mobutu stayed away from Kinshasa for much of 1991, when mass opposition grew.

When soldiers angry at not receiving a promised pay rise ran amok in Kinshasa in September 1991, France and Belgium sent in troops to protect foreign nationals and property. Looters ransacked supermarkets, factories and private homes.
At least 250 people died in the turmoil.

Surrounded by his Israeli-trained presidential guard, he spent most of his time in his opulent northern palace in Gbadolite, sometimes called "Versailles in the Jungle", hurling defiance at his opponents.

After the parliament's impeachment threat, he told Reuters he would pay no heed to the 450 councillors. "Since I am not answerable to them and I have nothing to do with them, I simply ignore them," he said.
The son of a cook and a hotel maid, Mobutu was born in Lisala in Equateur province on October 14, 1930. He is married to Bobila Dawa and the couple have 12 children.
